input.strategy_title: Default Vector Store for Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag
input.strategy_markdown:
## Summary

RHOAI must provide a default vector store that is available out-of-the-box — without manual setup — so that Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag continue to function when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution image. Today these capabilities depend on an inline vector store provider bundled within the Llama Stack process; removing it (per RHAISTRAT-7474) will break them unless an alternative is available at the platform level.

## Problem Statement

Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag currently rely on an inline Milvus provider embedded in the Llama Stack distribution image to store and retrieve vector embeddings. This inline provider runs inside the Llama Stack process itself.

RHAISTRAT-7474 proposes removing inline providers from the Llama Stack distribution to improve GA readiness — shipping only what can be tested and maintained at scale, and aligning with Llama Stack's primary use case as a remote API server. However, no platform-level alternative exists today. If inline providers are removed without a replacement, any RHOAI user relying on Gen AI Studio's RAG capabilities or Auto Rag will lose functionality entirely — there is no workaround short of manually provisioning and configuring an external vector database.

Users expect vector storage to "just work" when they use Gen AI Studio or Auto Rag. The current out-of-the-box experience must be preserved even as the underlying architecture evolves.

## Affected Customers

* All RHOAI customers using Gen AI Studio playground with RAG capabilities
* All RHOAI customers using Auto Rag
* This is a platform-level product dependency: these features cannot function without a vector store

## Business Justification

* **Product integrity:** Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag are GA-track capabilities in RHOAI. Removing the inline vector store without a replacement breaks shipped product functionality for every user of these features.
* **Blocking dependency:** RHAISTRAT-7474 (removing inline providers for GA readiness) cannot proceed until this RFE is resolved. Silas Brenmark (Gen AI Studio lead) has identified this as a blocker.
* **User experience:** RHOAI differentiates on integrated, opinionated defaults. Requiring users to manually provision and configure a vector database before they can use the playground or Auto Rag degrades the out-of-the-box experience that customers expect from the platform.

## Acceptance Criteria

* \[ \] A default vector store is available out-of-the-box on RHOAI without requiring users to manually provision or configure external infrastructure
* \[ \] Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows function with the default vector store with no loss of current capability
* \[ \] Auto Rag functions with the default vector store with no loss of current capability
* \[ \] The default vector store runs as a separate process, decoupled from the Llama Stack instance (not an inline provider)
* \[ \] The default vector store is scoped appropriately for multi-tenant environments (e.g., per-namespace isolation)
* \[ \] The default vector store is lightweight enough to run in resource-constrained environments without imposing significant overhead

## Success Criteria

* Users of Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag experience no functional regression when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution
* No additional manual setup steps are required for RAG workflows compared to the current experience
* RHAISTRAT-7474 is unblocked and can proceed to implementation

## Open Questions

* What is the preferred scoping model — per namespace, per Llama Stack instance, or both? (Silas noted per-namespace is preferred for isolation, but Auto Rag may need per-instance scoping)
* Should users have a migration path from the default vector store to a production-grade vector database? (Bram Sundqvist raised the importance of aligning with commonly-used vector DB providers for easier migration)

## Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)

> **Note:** The full strategy exceeds Jira's description size limit and is stored as an attachment: `RHAISTRAT-8004-strategy.md`.

## Staff Engineer Input

**Correction 1 — OGX does not auto-provision PostgreSQL.** OGX defaults to SQLite for storage (`storage.kv.type: sqlite`, `storage.sql.type: sqlite` in the OGXServer CRD). The odh-dashboard gen-ai BFF hardcodes SQLite when creating OGXServer instances for the playground (`kv_sqlite` and `sql_sqlite` in `llamastack_config.go`). PostgreSQL is a supported backend but must be user-configured with an explicit `connectionString` secret. The strategy's claim that "every LlamaStackDistribution instance requires a PostgreSQL database" is incorrect — introducing PostgreSQL is new work, not an extension of existing infrastructure.

**Correction 2 — A Red Hat PostgreSQL image with pgvector already exists.** The `registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16` image includes pgvector out of the box — confirmed in the [sclorg/postgresql-container Dockerfile](https://github.com/sclorg/postgresql-container/blob/master/16/Dockerfile.rhel9) (`INSTALL_PKGS="$INSTALL_PKGS pgvector"`). PostgreSQL 18 (RHEL 9) also includes pgvector. Furthermore, the model-registry-operator already uses `postgresql-16` as its auto-provisioned database image, and `RELATED_IMAGE_POSTGRESQL_16_IMAGE` is already present in the rhods-operator CSV for disconnected installs. No custom image build is needed. No Konflux onboarding is needed. The 1-2 sprint image onboarding estimate in the strategy can be eliminated.

**Architectural direction — platform-level database vs. self-provisioned.** Multiple RHOAI components now need PostgreSQL (model-registry, MLflow, and now OGX for pgvector). The preferred long-term direction is a platform-provided shared PostgreSQL managed via the DSC, where each component consumes a connection string rather than self-provisioning. A shared platform-provided PostgreSQL via DSC will not be available until RHOAI 3.6. For 3.5, Gen AI Studio must provision its own PostgreSQL instance.

**Operator dependency for self-provisioning (RHAISTRAT-7164).** Self-provisioning PostgreSQL following the model-registry-operator pattern requires a RHOAI-controlled operator for Gen AI Studio. The ogx-k8s-operator is upstream and cannot carry RHOAI-specific provisioning logic. The dashboard operator modularization (RHAISTRAT-7164, In Progress) would provide this operator layer. This is a hard dependency — until RHAISTRAT-7164 delivers, there is no RHOAI-controlled operator where PostgreSQL lifecycle management can live. It will be challenging to commit this strategy to a specific release until that dependency is delivered.

**Fallback if RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time.** If the dashboard modularization is not ready for 3.5, the fallback is to require customers to bring their own PostgreSQL for RAG capabilities in the Playground. Users would manually configure the OGXServer CR spec with their PostgreSQL connection details. This aligns with the breaking changes introduced in OGX 1.0, even though the Playground largely abstracts OGX from users. The development team should define a go/no-go gate for this decision as part of sprint planning.

**Decouple from Auto Rag.** Auto Rag integration with Gen AI Studio (RHAISTRAT-7824) is targeting RHOAI 3.6. This strategy should validate pgvector only for Gen AI Studio Playground RAG workflows. Auto Rag compatibility with pgvector will be addressed in RHAISTRAT-7824's scope. Remove Auto Rag from affected components, impacted teams, acceptance criteria, and validation requirements.

**Performance and index thresholds — dev experimentation scope.** The default pgvector instance is meant for development experimentation, not production usage. Strict latency SLAs (p50/p95/p99) are not required. The sprint 1 benchmark should capture the inline Milvus baseline and verify pgvector is in the same order of magnitude, not meet a specific threshold. Typical Playground RAG usage involves small document sets — flat scan (no index) is sufficient for the default. Users with production-scale vector workloads should use an external vector database. Remove open questions about latency thresholds, corpus size ranges, and index type selection.

**PostgreSQL resource sizing.** Reference the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL resource requests/limits as the starting point. Adjust based on sprint 1 benchmarking if needed.

**Alternative fallback — BFF-managed PostgreSQL provisioning.** If RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time, an alternative to requiring customers to bring their own PostgreSQL is to have the gen-ai BFF provision the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance directly, similar to how the BFF currently provisions guardrails infrastructure. The BFF would create the PostgreSQL Deployment, Service, PVC, and Secret when a playground with RAG is configured, if one does not already exist in the namespace. Caveats: (1) the implementation must be designed for portability — when the platform-provided shared database becomes available (3.6), the BFF should consume the shared connection string rather than self-provisioning; (2) lifecycle management of the PostgreSQL instance must be carefully considered — the BFF is not an operator with a reconciliation loop, so cleanup on playground deletion, handling of pod restarts, and credential rotation need explicit design attention.

**Existing remote vector store implementation is reusable.** Per the engineering team, the existing remote vector store implementation can be largely reused for pgvector integration. The majority of the work effort is around infrastructure and provisioning of the PostgreSQL/pgvector database, not the vector_io provider integration itself.

**Correction 3 — Vector storage and application storage are independent configurations.** The OGX vector_io provider configuration (`remote::pgvector` via `ENABLE_PGVECTOR`) is completely separate from OGX's application storage backend configuration (`storage.kv.type`, `storage.sql.type`). This strategy only needs to configure the pgvector vector_io provider — it does not change the application storage backend, which remains on its existing default (SQLite). There is no SQLite-to-PostgreSQL migration concern because the application storage is not being touched. Remove any references to consolidating vector and application storage in a single database, and remove any SQLite-to-PostgreSQL upgrade path considerations.

# Operator-based self-provisioning of PostgreSQL/pgvector for Gen AI Studio (branch A)

## Description

Branch outcome A, executed if the go/no-go decision selects operator-based provisioning — i.e. the dashboard operator modularization (RHAISTRAT-7164) delivers a RHOAI-controlled operator for Gen AI Studio in time for the target release. This epic implements PostgreSQL lifecycle management in that operator layer, following the model-registry-operator's pattern of auto-provisioning a PostgreSQL database per managed instance. It uses the existing Red Hat PostgreSQL image with pgvector included (`registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16`); no custom image build or pipeline onboarding is needed.

## Scope

- Implement per-namespace PostgreSQL self-provisioning for playgrounds with RAG enabled, in the RHOAI-controlled operator layer, following the model-registry-operator pattern for auto-provisioned databases.
- Provision the existing Red Hat PostgreSQL 16 image (pgvector included) with generated credentials stored in a secret, exposed to the playground's OGXServer as the vector_io provider connection.
- Seed PostgreSQL resource requests/limits from the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL sizing as the starting point.
- Handle lifecycle via the operator reconciliation loop: cleanup on playground deletion, recovery on pod restarts, credential management.
- Keep the image reference resolvable for disconnected installs, reusing the platform's existing related-image mechanism for the PostgreSQL 16 image.
- Design for portability: when the platform-provided shared PostgreSQL becomes available (following release), consume the shared connection string instead of self-provisioning.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A playground with RAG configured in a namespace has a running, pgvector-enabled PostgreSQL instance provisioned without any user action beyond enabling the playground.
- The provisioned database's connection details are available to the OGX vector_io provider via a secret, and playground RAG workflows succeed end to end against it.
- Lifecycle behaviors are handled by reconciliation: deleting the playground cleans up the provisioned database; pod restarts and credential handling recover without manual intervention.
- PostgreSQL resource requests/limits are set from the model-registry-operator reference sizing, with any adjustments justified.
- The image reference is overridable for disconnected installs through the platform's existing related-image mechanism.
- The design documents the migration path to consuming the platform-provided shared database connection string when it becomes available.

## HLR Traceability

- AC-1 — a default vector store is available out-of-the-box without manual provisioning or configuration of external infrastructure.
- AC-4 — the vector store runs as a separate process (a standalone PostgreSQL deployment), decoupled from the OGX instance.
- AC-5 — scoped for multi-tenant environments via per-namespace isolation.
- AC-6 — lightweight enough for resource-constrained environments (sizing seeded from the reference operator).
- Staff Engineer directives: model-registry-operator pattern for self-provisioning; hard dependency on RHAISTRAT-7164 for the operator layer; existing RH PostgreSQL 16 image with pgvector; resource sizing reference.

# BFF-managed PostgreSQL/pgvector provisioning for Gen AI Studio (branch B)

## Description

Branch outcome B, executed if the go/no-go decision selects the fallback because the RHOAI-controlled operator layer (from the dashboard operator modularization, RHAISTRAT-7164) does not land in time for the target release. The gen-ai BFF provisions the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance directly when a playground with RAG is configured and no suitable database exists in the namespace — mirroring how the BFF already provisions guardrails infrastructure. It uses the existing Red Hat PostgreSQL image with pgvector included (`registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16`); no custom image build or pipeline onboarding is needed. Because the BFF is not an operator with a reconciliation loop, lifecycle management receives explicit design attention.

## Scope

- Implement idempotent provisioning in the gen-ai BFF: when a playground with RAG is configured and no suitable PostgreSQL instance exists in the namespace, create the PostgreSQL Deployment, Service, persistent storage, and credentials secret; reuse an existing instance when one is present.
- Wire the provisioned database's connection details into the OGX vector_io provider configuration the BFF already produces.
- Design and implement lifecycle management without a reconciliation loop: cleanup on playground deletion, handling of pod restarts, and credential rotation each get an explicit, tested design.
- Seed PostgreSQL resource requests/limits from the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL sizing as the starting point.
- Keep the image reference resolvable for disconnected installs, reusing the platform's existing related-image mechanism for the PostgreSQL 16 image.
- Design for portability: when the platform-provided shared PostgreSQL becomes available (following release), the BFF consumes the shared connection string rather than self-provisioning.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A playground with RAG configured in a namespace has a running, pgvector-enabled PostgreSQL instance provisioned without any user action beyond enabling the playground.
- Provisioning is idempotent: reconfiguring or restarting the playground does not duplicate or destroy the database; an existing suitable instance is reused.
- The provisioned database's connection details reach the OGX vector_io provider via a secret, and playground RAG workflows succeed end to end against it.
- Lifecycle behaviors are explicitly designed and tested: cleanup on playground deletion, recovery on pod restarts, and credential rotation behave as documented.
- PostgreSQL resource requests/limits are set from the model-registry-operator reference sizing, with any adjustments justified.
- The image reference is overridable for disconnected installs through the platform's existing related-image mechanism.
- The design documents the migration path to consuming the platform-provided shared database connection string when it becomes available.

## HLR Traceability

- AC-1 — a default vector store is available out-of-the-box without manual provisioning or configuration of external infrastructure.
- AC-4 — the vector store runs as a separate process (a standalone PostgreSQL deployment), decoupled from the OGX instance.
- AC-5 — scoped for multi-tenant environments via per-namespace isolation.
- AC-6 — lightweight enough for resource-constrained environments (sizing seeded from the reference operator).
- Staff Engineer directives: alternative fallback of BFF-managed provisioning modeled on the guardrails infrastructure pattern; portability to the shared platform database; explicit lifecycle design because the BFF has no reconciliation loop; existing RH PostgreSQL 16 image with pgvector.

# Go/no-go decision: PostgreSQL provisioning approach for the Gen AI Studio default vector store

## Description

This epic resolves the central open decision in the strategy: how the default pgvector-backed vector store's PostgreSQL database is provisioned for Gen AI Studio in the current release. Operator-based self-provisioning requires a RHOAI-controlled operator for Gen AI Studio, which the dashboard operator modularization effort (RHAISTRAT-7164, In Progress) is expected to provide; if that does not land in time for the target release, the fallback is BFF-managed provisioning in the gen-ai BFF. The Staff Engineer Input directs the development team to define a go/no-go gate for this decision as part of sprint planning. The outcome selects which provisioning implementation is executed and is recorded as a decision document.

## Scope

- Assess the delivery readiness and timeline of the dashboard operator modularization (RHAISTRAT-7164) against the target release dates.
- Define the go/no-go gate criteria and decision date in sprint planning, tied to the release milestone.
- Evaluate the two viable provisioning approaches against the strategy's requirements:
  - Out-of-the-box experience: no manual user provisioning or configuration.
  - Lifecycle management: cleanup on playground deletion, handling of pod restarts, credential rotation (a BFF is not an operator with a reconciliation loop, so these need explicit design attention).
  - Portability to the platform-provided shared PostgreSQL expected in the following release (consume a shared connection string rather than self-provision).
  - Per-namespace isolation for multi-tenant scoping.
- Record the selected approach, the evidence, and the impact of each outcome on the out-of-the-box requirement.
- Document the last-resort fallback — customers supplying their own PostgreSQL by configuring the OGXServer custom resource — including its user-facing impact, in case neither self-provisioning path is viable.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A written decision record identifies the selected provisioning approach and cites the evidence used (operator modularization delivery status, lifecycle-management trade-off analysis).
- Go/no-go gate criteria and a decision date are defined and agreed in sprint planning, anchored to the target release.
- The decision record documents, for each outcome, the impact on the out-of-the-box experience requirement.
- The last-resort fallback (customer-supplied PostgreSQL via OGXServer configuration) is documented with its user-facing impact.

## HLR Traceability

- Gates AC-1 (out-of-the-box default vector store) and AC-5 (multi-tenant scoping): the decision determines how per-namespace provisioning is delivered.
- Staff Engineer directives: hard dependency on RHAISTRAT-7164 for operator-based self-provisioning; go/no-go gate to be defined in sprint planning; fallback paths (BFF-managed provisioning, customer-supplied PostgreSQL).

# Configure the OGX pgvector vector_io provider for Gen AI Studio playground RAG

## Description

This epic wires Gen AI Studio playground RAG to use a remote pgvector-backed vector store, replacing the dependency on the inline Milvus provider that is being removed from the OGX distribution. The gen-ai BFF, which creates OGXServer instances for the playground, is extended to configure the OGX vector_io provider as remote pgvector, consuming PostgreSQL connection details from a secret. Per the Staff Engineer Input, the existing remote vector store implementation can be largely reused — the integration surface is configuration, not new provider code — and this work is independent of who provisions the database (the provider consumes a connection string under every provisioning approach).

## Scope

- Extend the gen-ai BFF's OGXServer instance creation so that a playground with RAG enabled configures the remote pgvector vector_io provider (via the OGX provider-activation mechanism, e.g. `ENABLE_PGVECTOR`), with connection details supplied from a Kubernetes secret.
- Reuse the existing remote vector store implementation for the pgvector integration.
- Scope the vector store per playground namespace (per-namespace isolation), matching the Staff Engineer's preferred scoping model.
- Leave the OGX application storage backend untouched on its existing default — vector storage and application storage are independent configurations; no SQLite-to-PostgreSQL migration is in scope.
- Ensure the configuration works for disconnected installs (no assumption of external image or dependency fetches beyond what the platform already references).
- Document guidance for users with production-scale vector workloads on pointing RAG at an external vector database (migration path off the dev-experimentation default).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A playground with RAG configured results in an OGXServer whose vector_io provider is the remote pgvector provider — not an inline provider — running as a separate process from the OGX instance.
- Vector insert, query, and delete operations through the playground RAG workflow succeed against a pgvector-backed instance with no loss of current capability.
- The provider consumes PostgreSQL connection details from a secret; no manual provider setup is required from the user beyond the database being reachable.
- The OGX application storage backend remains on its existing default (no application-storage migration).
- The vector store is scoped per playground namespace.
- The provider switch is reversible: the BFF can revert a playground to the previous inline-provider default (by disabling the pgvector provider activation, e.g. the `ENABLE_PGVECTOR` guard) while inline providers still exist in the distribution — i.e., before RHAISTRAT-7474 lands — with the playground returning to inline-provider RAG behavior.
- Documentation describes how users can configure an external, production-grade vector database for RAG workloads that outgrow the default.

## HLR Traceability

- AC-2 — Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows function with the default vector store with no loss of current capability (delivered by this epic; verified by the benchmark work).
- AC-4 — the default vector store runs as a separate process, decoupled from the OGX instance (remote provider, not inline).
- Staff Engineer Corrections 1 and 3 — OGX defaults to SQLite for application storage (PostgreSQL is new work, scoped to the provisioning decision); vector storage configuration is independent of application storage configuration.
- Staff Engineer directive / open question on migration path — resolved as documented guidance for external vector databases.

# Benchmark pgvector against the inline Milvus baseline and set PostgreSQL resource sizing

## Description

This epic delivers the sprint-1 benchmark the Staff Engineer Input calls for: capture the inline Milvus provider's baseline performance and verify that pgvector is in the same order of magnitude for typical Gen AI Studio playground RAG usage, then derive the PostgreSQL resource sizing for the default vector store. The default store is intended for development experimentation — strict latency SLAs are explicitly not required; the pass condition is order-of-magnitude parity, not a threshold. Typical playground RAG usage involves small document sets, for which a flat scan (no vector index) is sufficient.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A benchmark report records the inline Milvus baseline and the pgvector results for representative playground RAG workloads (small document sets, flat scan, insert and query paths).
- The benchmark runs against a standalone, self-provisioned pgvector PostgreSQL instance (existing platform-referenced image, seeded from the model-registry-operator's reference sizing); the benchmark does not depend on the default-provisioning path being delivered, and its setup is scripted and reproducible.
- Pgvector results are within the same order of magnitude as the inline Milvus baseline; deviations beyond that are escalated as findings rather than silently accepted.
- A resource sizing recommendation for the provisioned PostgreSQL instance is documented, seeded from the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL resource requests/limits, with any adjustments justified by the benchmark results.

## Scope

- Define and run a reproducible benchmark comparing the inline Milvus provider baseline against the remote pgvector provider through playground RAG workflows (document ingestion and retrieval).
- Use representative dev-experimentation workloads: small document sets, flat scan, no vector index selection, no corpus-size threshold studies.
- Capture the inline Milvus baseline before the inline provider is removed from the distribution, so the comparison is grounded.
- Self-provision a standalone benchmark PostgreSQL/pgvector instance — using the existing pgvector-enabled image already referenced by the platform (`registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16`), seeded from the model-registry-operator's reference sizing — rather than consuming the provisioned default. The benchmark is a sprint-1 deliverable and must be runnable before any default-provisioning path lands; the provisioning approach is selected independently and later.
- Produce the benchmark report and the PostgreSQL resource sizing recommendation (requests/limits), seeded from the model-registry-operator's sizing.

## HLR Traceability

- AC-2 — playground RAG functions with no loss of current capability: this epic is the measured verification of that criterion (order-of-magnitude parity with the inline baseline).
- AC-6 — the default vector store is lightweight enough for resource-constrained environments: verified through the resource sizing recommendation.
- Staff Engineer directives: performance and index thresholds are dev-experimentation scope (no SLAs, order-of-magnitude check, flat scan); resource sizing references the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL settings.

decomposition_quality 5/5 — SCORE: 5

## Dimension 1: HLR Coverage — solid

The strategy is real-tier with no HLR-N labels (full body in an unfetched attachment), so coverage must be traced to the prose ACs and staff input — and it is, exhaustively:

- AC-1 → branch epics; AC-2 → E002 (delivers) + E004 (verifies); AC-3 → explicitly descoped per Staff Engineer with the descope recorded in both the matrix and Health Warnings; AC-4 → E002 + branches; AC-5/AC-6 (the NFR-flavored criteria the annotations warned might be dropped) → branch epics + E004 sizing. All three success criteria have matrix rows; both open questions are resolved (scoping by SE direction with a revisit trigger; migration path folded into E002 as guidance).
- Priority inheritance holds: E001 (P0) gates the P0 branches; E004 is P1 and blocks nothing. The P1-epic-verifies-a-P0-AC inversion is disclosed in Health Warnings with rationale rather than hidden — the right way to handle it.
- Every Staff Engineer directive is logged as a numbered override in the summary (Corrections 1–3, DSC/3.6 portability, the 7164 dependency, fallbacks, Auto Rag decouple, dev-experimentation perf scope, sizing reference). Nothing orphaned.

## Dimension 2: Epic Boundaries — solid

The two branch epics build the same deliverable two ways but are mutually exclusive conditional branches (exactly one executes, `gate_failure_impact: remove`) — this is precisely the "decision point, not two parallel committed streams" shape the annotations call for. E002 (provider consumption) and the branches (secret production/provisioning) are complementary halves of one secret interface, not duplicate surfaces. Sizes are sprint-plausible (decision record, config wiring, scoped benchmark, pattern-mirroring provisioning). The single-team assignment is disclosed as relying on the strategy label given the missing Teams table — defensible, and the annotations warn against over-splitting a mostly single-team change. E002's migration-guidance doc item is a thin SE-directed resolved-open-question record, not content-authoring scale.

## Dimension 3: DAG Quality — solid

Mermaid arrows (dependency→dependent) match all frontmatter `dependencies` exactly; every edge and every deliberately absent edge (no E001→E002, no E002↔branches, no E004↔branches) is justified in the DAG Justification table with correct rule citations. The critical external dependency is handled exactly as the annotations demand: RHAISTRAT-7164 is modeled as an in-DAG Investigation gate (E001) plus Health Warnings — not a `gated_by` pointing outside the DAG, and none of 7164's work is absorbed (branch A builds *in* the operator layer, not the layer itself). Tiered delivery prevents falsely serializing E002 behind the decision. The one residual nit (branch epics' end-to-end ACs implicitly presume E002's wiring, with no prose note inside the branch files) is rule-compliant in shape — the construction rules forbid a configuration reference as a dependency edge — and the coordination is acknowledged at the summary level as merge risk. Sub-minor.

## Dimension 4: Scope Fidelity — solid

Every named mechanism traces to the source: `ENABLE_PGVECTOR`/`remote::pgvector`, `registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16`, the model-registry-operator pattern and sizing, the guardrails-provisioning precedent, related-image/CSV disconnected-install mechanism, per-namespace scoping, flat scan, the lifecycle concerns (cleanup/restarts/credential rotation). No invented API paths, CRD fields, env vars, or policies. E004's self-provisioned benchmark instance is a sound derivation (sprint-1 benchmark must run before any provisioning path lands), not invented detail. No epic body references sibling draft IDs; external keys (7474/7164/7824) are legitimate strategy references. Critically, none of the SE-invalidated work reappears: no image build, no Konflux/license/repo onboarding, no storage migration, no latency SLAs or index selection.

## Dimension 5: Acceptance Criteria — solid

All ACs are testable and traceable. E002 carries the rule-mandated reversibility AC for replacement work, grounded in the `ENABLE_PGVECTOR` guard and correctly time-boxed to before RHAISTRAT-7474 lands. E004's order-of-magnitude criterion matches the SE's explicit scope (with deterministic escalation handling for deviations) rather than dressing up SLAs. E001's "agreed in sprint planning" AC is a condition on the epic's own deliverable, which the SE input explicitly directs. Schedule risks (7164 timing, baseline capture window, release commitment) are correctly kept in Health Warnings/gate-failure text, not as soft ACs.

## Watch-list verification (annotation traps)

All nine traps are cleared: no hallucinated scope (Input Health discloses the missing attachment and keys traceability to ACs + SE input); SE corrections win; Auto Rag descoped *with the title/summary conflict explicitly noticed and flagged*; 7164 as in-DAG gate + health warning with no absorption; conditional branches with the non-engineering last resort (bring-your-own) as documented fallback rather than an epic; benchmark kept honest; no over-splitting; docs handled proportionately; multi-tenancy and resource-footprint criteria mapped.

The only deductions I can construct — the implicit E002 sequencing note in branch epics, E004 typed Implementation rather than Investigation (defensible: it produces a durable artifact and gates nothing, so Investigation gating semantics wouldn't fit), and the thin doc item in E002 — are each polish-level and each carries an explicit, reasonable rationale in the artifacts. The contract validator passed and the adversarial review found exactly one minor issue. All five dimensions are solid; this is a model handling of a trap-dense real strategy. | [informational] internal adversarial review score 14/14
